exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with fever and a history of nightly ITN use – what additional history questions clarify possible ITN failure? — Ask about net condition, correct hanging, sleeping location, and recent travel to high‑transmission areas.

Explain why a patient on an ITN may still develop severe malaria — — Insecticide resistance, net damage, or inconsistent use can allow bites; parasite load may still become high enough to cause severe disease.

How would you counsel a pregnant woman on ITN use and why is it especially important? — — Emphasize nightly use, proper hanging, and that ITNs reduce maternal anaemia and low birth weight; pregnancy increases susceptibility to malaria.

What public‑health indicator would you use to evaluate the success of an ITN distribution campaign? — — Household coverage ≥80 % and reduction in malaria incidence or EIR over the following transmission season.

A clinic lacks malaria RDTs; how do you manage a febrile child who sleeps under an ITN? — — Use WHO clinical algorithm: assess for danger signs, treat presumptively if severe, arrange referral, and consider empirical antimalarial if high transmission season.

Describe the mechanism of action of the pyrethroid used in ITNs and a key safety consideration. — — Pyrethroids prolong sodium channel opening causing neuronal hyper‑excitation in insects; they are safe for humans at net concentrations but can cause dermatitis in sensitive individuals.

What are the main reasons for switching from conventional ITNs to long‑lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs)? — — LLINs retain insecticide after 20+ washes, reduce need for re‑impregnation, and maintain efficacy for 3–5 years.

Identify a situation where ITNs alone are insufficient for malaria control and what adjunctive measure is recommended. — — In areas with high outdoor biting or resistance, combine ITNs with indoor residual spraying or larval source management.
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Insecticide‑treated bed nets (ITNs) are a key vector‑control tool that reduces malaria transmission and other mosquito‑borne diseases. Understanding their use, effectiveness, and limitations is essential for clinicians in low‑resource settings.

b: Reduces malaria incidence by ~50 % in endemic areas
Effective against Anopheles, Aedes and Culex species
Long‑lasting nets retain efficacy for 3–5 years
sections.p: ITNs are mosquito nets impregnated with a pyrethroid insecticide. They provide both a physical barrier and a chemical kill effect, protecting sleepers throughout the night.

b: Coverage goal: ≥80 % of households with at least one net per two people
Net integrity: holes >2 cm compromise protection
Insecticide resistance: monitor local vector susceptibility
sections.p: The protective benefit of ITNs depends on proper coverage, correct hanging, and regular replacement when the insecticide loses potency.

b: Ask about nightly net use during history taking
Inspect net condition in the home if possible
Consider alternative prophylaxis if resistance is documented
sections.p: Clinicians must assess net use when evaluating febrile patients, counsel on proper handling, and recognize that ITN failure may present as breakthrough malaria.
